This allows for better organization and encapsulation of code into modules, improving security and maintainability. Java 9 also introduced the `var` keyword for local variable type inference, simplifying code.

answersA.title: Java 8 vs Java 9 example
answersA.text: Here's an example of a key difference between Java 8 and Java 9: Java 9 introduced the `try-with-resources` statement to automatically close resources that implement the `AutoCloseable` interface. For instance, in Java 8, you might manually close a stream, but in Java 9, you can use `try-with-resources` to ensure it's closed even if errors occur.

answersC.title: Java 8 vs Java 9 example
answersC.text: Here is a concrete example of a difference between Java 8 and Java 9. In Java 9, the `Stream` API was enhanced with the `takeWhile` and `dropWhile` methods. For instance, `takeWhile` will take elements from a stream as long as a condition is true, and stop as soon as it becomes false. This contrasts with Java 8's `filter`, which processes all elements and only keeps those matching the predicate.

answersC.title: Java 8 vs Java 9 example
answersC.text: In Java 9, the `Optional` class gained new methods like `ifPresentOrElse`. This allows you to provide a default action if the `Optional` is empty, which can make code cleaner than traditional `if/else` checks. For example, you could use `optionalValue.ifPresentOrElse(System.out::println, () -> System.out.println("Value not present"));` to print the value if it exists, or a message indicating its absence.
